When a session has changed something, x3 waits until it has been quiet for 15 minutes, or until you disconnect, and saves the router's configuration as text. Each router gets its own folder, and an export identical to the last one is not stored again.

The export is read straight off the router's console: nothing is written to its flash, and a session that changes nothing takes no snapshot at all.

With audit on, every request x3 sends and every reply the router gives back is written to a file as it happens: what was changed, when, and what the router answered. It is the answer to "what did I actually do to this device?", and the file can be read back, listed and diffed with x3ctl audit FILE.

x3 reads each router's own schema, so its menus, lists and forms are the ones the device describes. A few things it does on its own are worth deciding up front: how a change reaches the router, the config snapshots it can keep for you, and the audit record it can write of every connection.

If you have used the official client, the menus and forms will feel familiar, because they come from the same router. The pages ahead are mostly about what x3 adds on top.

The next pages explain each one and let you switch it on or off. Everything here can be changed later, and this tour can be reopened from Help ▸ Welcome Tour.

x3 reads the address book the official client saves (Addresses.cdb), so the routers you already saved are listed on the first start. It never rewrites that file: notes, groups and passwords you change in x3 go to an overlay of its own.
